lead: An HTML page is a text file. The browser reads it and builds a tree of elements in memory. Tags mark where an element begins and ends; attributes in the start tag tune it. The skeleton — doctype, html, head, body — keeps page information apart from page content. Every screen in this subject sits on it: the notice board below, the forms of chapter 2.3, and the React components of Unit 5, which reach the browser as ordinary HTML.
prereq: You need: how a browser fetches a URL over HTTP and where the developer console lives (Unit 1, Internet, World Wide Web and DNS; Unit 1, Developer tools: VS Code, Git and browser consoles).

sections.h3: The skeleton: doctype, html, head and body

blocks.text: An HTML file is plain text. The browser reads it from top to bottom and builds a tree of elements in memory. The same skeleton opens every page you will write.

blocks.code:
Notices

Notice: the exam is today.

blocks.text: The first line is the doctype: an exclamation mark, the word DOCTYPE, and the word html. It is not an element and has no closing tag. It tells the browser to use modern standard rules, not an old compatibility mode whose default sizes differ, so a page without it can look slightly wrong even when the markup is fine.
html is the root element; every other element sits inside it. Its lang attribute names the language of the text — en for English, ta for Tamil — and screen readers and spell checkers use it.

head holds information about the page, not content the reader sees. Several things live there. title is the text on the browser tab and in a bookmark. meta with charset="UTF-8" declares the character set; without it, the rupee sign ₹ or a Tamil letter can appear as garbage. meta with name="viewport" and content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1" tells a phone to use its real width, which responsive layout needs (chapter 2.8). link with rel="stylesheet" attaches an external CSS file. A script element with a src attribute loads JavaScript the same way.
body holds everything visible: headings, paragraphs, images, forms.

sections.h3: Tag, element, attribute — three different words

blocks.text: A tag is markup you type: the element name inside angle brackets. The name alone is a start tag; the name after a slash is an end tag. Tags are punctuation, nothing more.

An element is the whole unit: start tag, content, end tag. A paragraph element is the start tag, the sentence, and the end tag together. Elements nest; an element inside another is its child, the outer one its parent.

An attribute is a name="value" pair inside the start tag. In an a element, href gives the destination and target="_blank" opens it in a new tab. The head's link element also uses href, but there it names the file being attached, and it has no target attribute. Double quotes are the convention and single quotes also work. Leave quotes on. An unquoted value cannot contain spaces, quotes, =, less-than or greater-than signs, or a backtick, and cannot be empty.

Void elements have no content and no end tag. Six appear constantly: br (line break), hr (horizontal rule), img (image), input (form field), meta and link. In img, input, meta and link the data arrives through attributes; br and hr simply mark a break or a rule, and their attributes only tune it. A stray end tag for one is quietly ignored.

A comment starts with <!-- and ends with -->, for example <!-- notice board starts here -->. It shows nothing on the page, but it is still a node in the DOM tree and you will see it in the Elements panel. It is not counted when you count elements.
Tag names are case-insensitive: upper case and lower case names give the same element. Write them in lower case, because that is the convention and the only form XHTML allows.

Global attributes work on every element. id gives one unique name per page. class gives a space-separated list of names many elements may share. style carries inline CSS. title shows a tooltip on hover. lang marks a language change inside the page.

sections.h3: The page is a tree, not a list

blocks.text: Nesting makes the document a tree. html is the root. head and body are its two children. title, meta and link are children of head. h1 and p are children of body. The em is a child of the p.
Two nesting rules matter. A child must close before its parent closes. And a p cannot contain another p or a heading; the browser ends the first paragraph and starts a new one without asking.

Browsers repair bad markup silently: a missing end tag, a closed void element, a paragraph inside a paragraph. The screen often looks right while the tree is wrong, and the CSS and JavaScript you add later act on the wrong tree. To see the repaired tree, right-click the page and choose Inspect, then the Elements panel. If the panel disagrees with your file, your markup is wrong. A validator such as the Nu HTML Checker lists the same faults.

examples.question: Write the smallest valid HTML5 page for a college notice board. It must have the document title "Notices", a level-1 heading "Notices", one paragraph in which the word "today" is emphasised, and a link to an external stylesheet. Draw the element tree and count the total elements, the void elements and the non-void elements.
steps: Line 1: doctype. Not an element, not counted.
Close head and open body. Count = 6.
p containing text and an em around today. p makes 8, em makes 9.
Close p, body and html. Tree: html at root, head and body as children, title, meta and link under head, h1 and p under body, em under p.
Total elements = 1 html + 1 head + 1 title + 1 meta + 1 link + 1 body + 1 h1 + 1 p + 1 em = 9.
examples.answer: The page has 9 elements in total: 7 non-void elements (html, head, title, body, h1, p, em) and 2 void elements (meta and link).
examples.check:
elements = ["html", "head", "title", "meta", "link", "body", "h1", "p", "em"]
void = {"meta", "link"}
total = len(elements)
void_count = len(void)
non_void = total - void_count
print(total)
print(non_void)
print(void_count)

traps: Mixing up title and h1. title is the browser tab and belongs in head; h1 is the visible heading and belongs in body. Examiners show a page with a heading but a blank tab and ask what is missing.

Closing a void element, as in an img or meta with an end tag. A trailing slash in an image start tag is allowed; a separate end tag for img is the error. The page often looks correct and the error surfaces only in the validator.
Nesting a p inside a p, or a heading inside a p. The browser closes the outer paragraph early, so the tree and element count differ from what you wrote.
Counting the doctype or a comment as an element. Neither is an element, so neither is counted in the element tree.
Forgetting meta charset and then displaying ₹ or an Indian-language word. The page loads but the characters come out as garbage.

quiz.q: Name the three parts that make up an element.
quiz.a: A start tag, the content, and an end tag. Void elements have only the start tag because their data is in attributes.

quiz.q: List four void elements and say what makes them void.
quiz.a: Any four of br, hr, img, input, meta, link. They have no content and no end tag. In img, input, meta and link data arrives through attributes; br and hr just mark a break or rule.

quiz.q: Why does title belong in head while h1 belongs in body?
quiz.a: head holds page information the browser uses but does not display; title is the tab and bookmark name. body holds visible content; h1 is part of that content.

quiz.q: Explain the difference between id and class as global attributes.
quiz.a: id names one element and must be unique on the page. class is a space-separated list of names shared by many elements, so a class selects a group.

quiz.q: Count the elements, void elements and non-void elements in this body: a body element containing an h1, a p that holds an em and a br, and an img. Show the counts.
quiz.a: body, h1, p, em, br, img = 6 elements. Void: br and img = 2. Non-void: 6 − 2 = 4.

quiz.q: A student writes a p element inside another p element. The page displays as intended. Explain what the browser did and why the problem can still bite later.
quiz.a: The browser found the second p start tag while a p was open, so it closed the first p and opened a sibling paragraph. The tree has two sibling paragraphs, not a nested pair. CSS for a p inside a p will never match, and a script walking the tree finds a different structure from the source.

quiz.q: A page shows the heading "Notices" correctly but the tab shows the file name instead of "Notices", and the rupee sign appears as strange characters. Name the two faults and the fix.
quiz.a: title is missing from head, or empty, so the browser shows the file name or URL. charset is missing or wrong, so the browser misreads ₹. Fix: add a non-empty title and put <meta charset="UTF-8"> as the first child of head.

beyond: Not for the exam. HTML is maintained as a continuously updated standard, not numbered versions, so HTML5 mostly means the current standard. Custom elements let you define your own tag names in JavaScript; this is how Web Components package a widget with its markup and behaviour. Search "custom elements" and "shadow DOM" next. Browsers expose the repaired tree to scripts through the DOM, which Unit 3 builds on. A validator in the build pipeline catches structural errors the screen hides.
